extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of American government and politics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts standards, elements, advantages, criticisms, and statutory controls relating to party organization, direct primary elections, conventions, and campaign finance as presented in a textbook on state and local politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element: Primary election within each party at stated time
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary election within each party at a stated time previous to each regular election, for the purpose of enabling party voters to express their choice among aspirants for nomination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a defining element of the direct primary system: a separate pre-election restricted to party voters to select party nominees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element: Methods for placing aspirants' names on the primary ballot
rubrics_metrics.description: Some method whereby party members who aspire to nomination may have their names placed upon the official ballot used at the primary election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described methods include: (a) petition (fixed number or percentage of party voters) — criticized for expense and burden on the poor; (b) payment of a filing fee varying by office; (c) party committees designating 'official' aspirants while allowing petition candidates; (d) certificate of designation by a designating assembly (Colorado model) which gives designated candidates preferred ballot position; (e) personal application without fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element: Determining order of names on the primary ballot
rubrics_metrics.description: Some method must be devised for determining the order in which names appear on the primary ballot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alphabetical order gives advantage to some names; practices to mitigate this include 'rotating' names so each aspirant appears at top on a portion of ballots, or ordering by time of filing (which is objectionable because it creates scramble outside filing offices). Rotation is noted as increasingly favored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element: Official printing and status of primary ballots
rubrics_metrics.description: Printing party primary ballots at public expense and making them as 'official' as the regular ballot used at elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practice has been established to produce uniform official primary ballots provided by public authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element: Determining the vote threshold to constitute nomination
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to determine what vote shall be required to constitute a choice at the primary (plurality vs majority; runoff/second ballot; percentage thresholds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most laws declare the highest vote-getter the nominee (allowing plurality/minority winners), but this is criticized. Remedies include: (a) requiring an absolute majority and holding a runoff between top two if none achieves it (common in the South); (b) threshold rules (Iowa 1907: highest with at least 35% otherwise convention nomination); (c) preferential/instant-runoff systems (Idaho: first- and second-choice voting, combine first and second-choice if no majority; Wisconsin variant: eliminate lowest and redistribute until someone has a majority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Element: Assembly (or mechanism) to formulate party platform
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to have an assembly of some kind to formulate the principles and issues of the party into a platform preparatory to the election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where conventions are omitted by primary law, platform drafting may be left to nominees working with officers, to a party committee, or to bodies like a party council; the convention method is praised but no fully satisfactory substitute has been found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element: Publicity pamphlet to equalize candidate publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision (as in Oregon) for a publicity pamphlet issued and sent to party members by public authorities, in which each aspirant may present claims for nomination by paying a sum proportioned to office size for use of a certain number of pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is intended to offset advantage from press advertising by wealthy or well-connected candidates; it is a mechanism to promote equality among aspirants in access to voters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element: Scope of application of direct primary to offices
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the direct primary applies to offices varies — from universal state-wide application to restriction to local offices, with some exemptions such as judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Western states tended to apply primaries to all elective offices; some states retained conventions for state offices (e.g., New York 1912); some laws exempt judges and use petition nomination instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage claimed: Encourages rank-and-file political activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct primaries encourage active political work by the rank and file by making it easier for ordinary party members to exercise influence in choosing committeemen and candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a democratic benefit of direct nomination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage claimed: Increases primary turnout and public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct primaries bring out a larger vote to the primaries than the older system of electing only convention delegates, indicating greater public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher participation in primaries is viewed as desirable to cultivate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage claimed: Prevents corporate control of nominations
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct primaries prevent powerful economic interests (railways, corporations) from contributing heavily to campaign expenses and controlling nominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seen as reducing special-interest domination of party machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage claimed: Secures democratic control and prevents machine domination
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct primaries secure democratic control within the party and prevent it from becoming an organized self-perpetuating machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democratic internal party control is a central normative justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage claimed: Promotes nomination of better candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: By making nomination depend upon presentation of claims to voters rather than secret manipulations, primaries secure the nomination of better men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumes voter scrutiny yields superior candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: Officeholders' quality not improved
rubrics_metrics.description: The personnel of the office-holding class has not been improved — better, more capable, and cleaner men have not been elected; civil service not improved by primaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue that primaries have not realized promised improvements in public office quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: Increased campaign money and corruption allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Public morals are not elevated; more money is expended in campaigns; many open charges of corruption and unlawful use of money have occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary contests are described as expensive and associated with corruption charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: Disorganization of parties and rise of personal machines
rubrics_metrics.description: Primaries have disorganized parties and built up personal political machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues primaries fragment party cohesion and institutional party structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: Legislative fragmentation and factionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the state legislature are split into factions, producing useless and sometimes harmful legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary-induced factionalism undermines legislative effectiveness and party responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: Expense bars poor candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: Poor men and men of moderate means cannot become candidates in contested primaries except by risking ruin or accepting financial aid (with obligations undesirable for public servants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petition requirements and campaign costs create economic barriers to entry; Oregon's expense limits and public pamphlet are offered as mitigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: Voters limited to self-nominated candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: Electors cannot 'vote directly for the men of their choice' at a primary because they must choose from names appearing on the primary ticket — typically those who circulated nomination papers or caused them to be circulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary ballots may present only self-nominated candidates, narrowing genuine voter choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: Bitterness and continual realignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary contests have engendered great bitterness, causing each election to produce new alignments of personal political machines and enmities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of collegial party rivalry; heightened acrimony in politics is a cost of primaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: Large public cost with little benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost of operating the primary system to taxpayers (state, counties, cities) has been enormous without corresponding benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial externalities of primaries are cited as a major drawback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: Incumbency advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: The law gives a decided advantage to the man in office — familiar officeholders or well-advertised candidates often win over better but less-known challengers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primaries may favor incumbents and those with media/profile advantages, undermining equal opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: Petition circulation industry
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing names on primary tickets by petition has created an industry of paid petition circulators and a market for procuring signatures, replacing earlier party clubs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercialization of nomination petitions is criticized as exchanging 'patriotism for pay.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: Abolition of conventions reduces political education
rubrics_metrics.description: Abolishing conventions has deprived party voters of opportunities to meet, exchange views, educate young politicians, and make 'trades' advantageous to the party ticket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conventions are characterized as schools of politics that foster acquaintance and practical political education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: Platforms made by candidates are ineffective
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms drafted by conventions composed of candidates for office (or substitutes where conventions are abolished) are often mere 'catch-vote' affairs and fail to represent party principles; candidates often ignore them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform-making mechanisms in the primary era are criticized for lack of seriousness and follow-through.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: Primaries have not eliminated political bosses
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary law has not dethroned the political boss; it may have merely changed the form of boss domination and increased opportunities for manipulation due to more complicated politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex political processes created by primaries require leadership and can increase boss activity rather than diminish it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision: When direct primary not applied, conventions nominate under regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominations for offices to which the direct primary is not applied are left to party conventions, which are regulated as to selection of delegates, conduct of meetings, and modes of procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws require notice of primaries for delegates, indicate which officers will be nominated by conventions, and generally stipulate that primaries for delegates be conducted like other primaries (polling places, hours).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: Convention procedures and protections (New York example)
rubrics_metrics.description: New York law defines 'convention' broadly and prescribes detailed rules: delegates chosen at primaries, apportionment of delegates by party vote, ample meeting room seating, call to order by committee chairman, specified general procedure, provisions for deciding contests over seats, delivery of certificates of election, and court review of actions with consideration but not control by party rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This entry encapsulates statutory procedural safeguards for conventions: formalization of delegate apportionment, notice, venue capacity, procedural formality, and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control category: Legislative approaches to control party finances
rubrics_metrics.description: Four distinct types of statutory provisions have been devised to control party financial operations: (a) regulation of candidates' expenditures; (b) definition and limitation of financial powers of committees; (c) restriction or prohibition of corporation contributions; (d) definition of objects for which money may be spent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four categories summarize legislative tendencies in campaign finance regulation (illustrated chiefly by New York statutes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory rule: Restrictions on candidates' expenditures and disclosure (New York)
rubrics_metrics.description: New York law limits the amount each candidate may spend and compels filing within twenty days after the election of a sworn statement detailing all receipts and expenditures; failure is a misdemeanor and may be punishable by forfeiture of office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Candidate spending limits plus mandatory post-election disclosure are enforcement mechanisms tied to criminal and administrative penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory rule: Control and accounting requirements for political committees (New York)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political committees must have a treasurer who keeps detailed accounts of receipts, promises, expenditures and liabilities; payments over $5 require vouchers; within twenty days after election a detailed statement must be filed listing amounts, sources, recipients, dates, and purposes (except transfers to other committees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treasurer duty, voucher requirement, and detailed disclosure aim to make committee finances transparent and auditable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory rule: Prohibition of corporation contributions (New York and federal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Law (New York 1906 amendment and federal law 1907) forbids corporations and joint-stock associations from directly or indirectly contributing money or property to parties, committees, or candidates; violation is a misdemeanor with prison and fine; officers/agents may be punished and immunity for testimony is provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute prohibition on corporate political contributions with criminal penalties and testimonial immunity to aid enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory rule: Definition of permitted objects of campaign expenditures (New York)
rubrics_metrics.description: The New York statute specifies permitted objects for campaign spending (rent of halls, expenses of public meetings, preparation/publication of 'literary material', compensation for agents preparing articles/ads, payment for newspaper publications, rent of offices/club rooms, compensation of clerks/agents/attorneys, lists of voters, personal/traveling expenses of candidates, compensation of poll workers, hire of carriages, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed enumeration aims to close loopholes but may still leave avenues for circumvention according to experienced election workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative experiment: State-funded campaign expense system (Colorado 1909)
rubrics_metrics.description: Colorado law (1909) declared campaign expenses for state, district, and county general elections to be paid only by the state and by the candidates; it made it a felony for others to contribute or for candidates/committees to accept such contributions, and regulated candidates' personal expenditures based on office salary/fees while providing state payments to parties per vote to be distributed by party chairmen under bond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A unique experiment to control private contributions by substituting state funds and limiting private spending, with severe criminal sanctions for violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary mechanics: Preferential/second-choice voting and elimination methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferential voting systems require voters to indicate first and second choices when many candidates run; an absolute majority of first-choice votes is required to nominate; if none receives a majority, second-choice votes are canvassed and combined or candidates with fewest votes are successively eliminated and their votes redistributed until someone has a majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idaho (1909) and Wisconsin (1911) are cited as examples: Idaho combines first/second choices; Wisconsin uses successive elimination and redistribution (instant-runoff style) until majority achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary procedural requirement: Primaries for delegates held like other primaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Primaries held for choosing delegates must be conducted like other primaries at regular polling places kept open a stipulated time; when delegates chosen are to form conventions for larger districts, county party conventions must be held the same day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures uniformity and coordination in delegate selection procedures to facilitate subsequent conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform-drafting institutional options (state law examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: States have created institutional mechanisms for drafting party platforms where conventions are curtailed: Wisconsin leaves it to meetings of candidates and certain officials; Kansas creates a party council composed of nominated candidates, national committeemen, certain senators, and county chairmen charged with drafting the state platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate statutory approaches to preserving party doctrine formulation when direct primaries replace traditional conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review of party convention actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are empowered to uphold rights secured by statute relating to conventions and to review actions or neglects related to conventions; in doing so the court shall consider but not be controlled by party rules and shall make such decision as justice requires under the facts and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute provides a legal remedy and standard for judicial oversight of party convention irregularities, including service of process on chairman or secretary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical observation: Ballot order effects favor top-listed candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical experience shows that candidates who appear near the top of the ballot (due to alphabetical order) have an actual advantage over those with later names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This observation motivates rotating ballot order or other corrective measures to ensure fairness among candidates.
